title: Say It to My Face
logline: Becca has a question, Professor Hale throws a dinner party at the edge of a cliff, and for one long Saturday Jack is exactly the friend Lena needs.

previously.text: On All Souls, Wes ended it on the phone. Lena, on the stairs: he said she’d marry him anyway, so he couldn’t let her.
At dawn on the stairs you decided to wait. She wants to be asked — and you don’t ask anybody the night her house falls down.
“Jack. What are you going to do?” “Whatever you need.” “I know. You always do.”
Theo’s mother asked how long you and Lena had been together. “We’re not — Becca’s with me.” Becca: “He’s *mine*!” Lena: “Nobody’s, as of last night.”
Your first night, Lena read the back of your postcard twice and asked who A.H. was, like she didn’t care.

s01.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:05 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Noon comes straight down on Portolá Hall, white and total, the kind of November light California hands out for free and Jack, on five hours of sleep for the second night running, would like to give back. Behind the front steps the lounge window is propped open on a phone book, and somebody’s laptop on the sill is playing the song with the ukulele that has been coming out of every window on campus since August — a little too much of it, and sweet, and hard to hold a grudge against. Through the glass the lounge TV is already on ESPN, warming up for tonight’s Game Six. In Youngstown the Yankees are something that happens to other people. Jack keeps up the family position.

Becca is on the top step with her knees up and her clipboard across them, ten minutes early because she is always ten minutes early. Beside her on the concrete are two coffees from the Portolá dining hall and a maple bar in wax paper: his order, memorized for Coffee & Donuts since the bleachers. Her braid is over one shoulder. The rosary on her wrist ticks against the paper cup when she hands him his.

The spiral planner is clipped on top, open to the week, and in the corner of today she has penciled *St. Charles Borromeo*. “Patron of catechists,” she says, “and *plague*. That’s a lot of hats for one guy.”
The coffee is too welcome. He drinks a third of it on his feet, and then he sits down on the step beside her, because she has moved her bag to make the room.

body.text: She doesn’t warm up to it. She has never warmed up to anything in her life. “You told Theo’s *mom* I’m with you,” she says. “In front of *everybody*. With the good forks.” She has been carrying it since last night, and it’s all over her face. “So — my mom’s been calling you my boyfriend since September. Can I tell her she’s right?”

body: Then, because there is a procedure for everything and she is generally the one who wrote it, she holds up a finger. “My mom first. Then Facebook. That’s the order.”

The rest of the plan comes with it: she flies home the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, Santa Barbara to Spokane through Seattle, and her dad will drive over from Coeur d’Alene to get her with the dog in the truck, and her mother has already named the turkey. “Gerald.” She says it gravely. “We don’t name the ones we eat. Mom says this is a teaching moment.”
“And you?” she says. “Thanksgiving?”
“Greyhound,” Jack says. “Two and a half days. Three if Chicago goes wrong.”
Becca frowns at that the way she frowns at a heifer lying down wrong, and writes BUS?? in the margin of the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, small, for later.

The sun is on her clipboard and on St. Charles in pencil and on her face, which is turned up to him with everything in it out where he can see it, nothing kept back for later. In the window the song gets to the part where it says the same thing over again. Jack holds the coffee. It’s hot through the paper, and he holds it.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned.

response: “Okay! *Yes!*” The phone is out of her vest pocket and dialing Coeur d’Alene while the ukulele is still going. “It’s noon there too,” she tells him with it at her ear. “North Idaho’s Pacific. People never believe me. — Mom. *Mom.* He said yes.”

Out of the little phone, small and clear, comes a woman’s voice: “Is that *him*? Put him on.” Becca holds it out. Jack takes it and says hello to a woman who has been calling him her daughter’s boyfriend since September, and Mrs. Lindell tells him she has had him on her list since the beach cleanup and wants to know if he’s eating, and he says yes, ma’am, and beside him on the step Becca puts her forehead down on the clipboard and laughs into St. Charles Borromeo.

body: Room 302 sounds like a Wednesday: fourteen chairs dragged across eighty-year-old oak, Caleb’s highlighter squeaking down a page of Boethius beside his copy of *The Consolations of Disbelief*, so full of Post-its it has started to molt, and Yusuf capping and uncapping his pen in a rhythm only he can hear. Hale comes in at one o’clock exactly, his fifth punctual arrival of the term, and he is in a good mood. He says good afternoon to each of them by surname, all the way around the table, and nobody trusts it.

Two seats down, in the cardigan, Lena takes one of the San Diego boys apart over whether Lady Philosophy is a woman or a device. It’s a small point. She goes at it with more than it needs, sleeves shoved up, and has it won in three moves, and Hale sits back with his hands laced on his stomach and lets her.

Under Jack’s notebook are her two pages from Monday, on Monica and on Lucille and the medal that came back in a plastic bag, red all through from the small hours of Wednesday, after the Anchor let him go at one, his handwriting getting smaller as the white ran out. One margin left: beside her last paragraph, where Monica at Ostia asks to be remembered at the altar and Lena’s grandmother comes into the argument by the side door, unannounced. Hale wants them by two. At ten to, with the San Diego boy still examining his injuries, Jack uncaps the red pen.

response: He writes it small, in the last of the white beside her last line. At two the papers go up the table hand to hand, and his comes up from Lena’s end with one page’s corner folded down — a dog-ear, small and square and made on purpose. Hale knocks it into the stack without looking. That is all Jack is going to see of whatever she wrote under it.

body: 412 is a war room the afternoon after the war. Laney is on her knees by the window in her PI LAM LITTLE shirt with the Martinelli’s out of the mini-fridge, gold bow and all, working the foil off the neck. In the corner stands the silk ficus Delphine left behind after the party, collecting dust in its pot since Saturday. Laney tips the bottle over the fake moss and pours.
“It’s dead anyway,” she says.
“It’s *silk*, Laney,” says Theo, from his desk.

“Then it can take it.” The cider fizzes down into the moss with a sound like applause in another building. Laney looks up at Jack over the bottle. “The judges,” she informs him, “have some notes on your interview.” Then she goes back to watering.

Theo has the fan of cream place cards from Tuesday morning on his blotter, the Harbor Inn’s, a little blue anchor in every corner — the first draft, with COSTIGAN · BROUSSARD side by side at the end of it — and he is tearing them up. Halves, then quarters, then eighths, laid in a neat white drift. When he has finished he brushes off his palms, stands, crosses the room and shakes Jack’s hand, perfectly.
“Congratulations, Costigan. She’s a wonderful girl.”
Jack looks at the ficus. It looks wet.

Kevin is in the doorway in the navy quarter-zip, zipped to the chin, backpack on one shoulder, taking it in: the cider in the moss, the snow on Theo’s blotter. “Respectfully,” he says. “Leave it alone.” Behind him Margot comes down the hall from the lounge in black with a paper cup of coffee in each hand, and on her way by she puts one of them into Kevin’s hand without stopping or saying a word, and goes on toward the stairs with the other.
Kevin stands there holding it, the steam going up past his collar, until Theo hooks the spare desk chair out with his foot, still looking at his blotter, and Kevin comes in and sits.

s04.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:04 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 2ND-FLOOR LANDING
body: The east stairwell runs on one caged bulb to a landing, a yellow like weak tea, and at the second floor the window is open its six inches onto the dark and the cold off the Lagoon.
Lena is on the step above the landing in sweatpants and the cardigan, with her LG closed in her lap. She looks up when he comes around the turn of the stair.
“I know,” she says. “It’s stupid.”

Jack sits one step below her, on the wall side, and puts his back against the cinderblock and says nothing. The phone stays shut in her lap. At 8:05 somebody on the third floor flushes, and the pipe in the wall behind Jack’s shoulder carries it all the way down to the basement, unhurried, like a man reading the minutes. Then 8:06. A moth has found the gap at the bottom of the window and is working out what to do about it. Everything Jack has to say is either wise or funny, and she has told him this week what to do with both. He stays. It’s the only other thing he has.
She says it once, at seven past. “He’d have called from the boat. He always said the boat had the best reception in Orleans Parish.” She turns the phone over in her lap. “It didn’t.”

Down on the ground floor a door bangs, and somebody laughs, and the laugh goes off into the lobby. She has moved the phone off her lap onto the step beside her, and she sits with her arms around her shins in the yellow light, eighteen years old and from a long way off, and Jack sits with her.
Some time after that, out of nowhere, she tells him she hasn’t opened her laptop since Monday. It’s been on her desk with the lid shut for two days. “Everybody I’ve ever met is on there being sorry.”
Jack still has the Portolá steps on him, the coffee and the noon sun, and a question he carried down two flights.

choices.text: “Becca asked me something today. I said yes.”
choices.key: On the landing at 8:04, the hour that used to be Wes’s, you told Lena about Becca yourself.
response: “I’m happy for you, Jack.” Her hand goes to the medal at her collar. “I mean it.”
Then she asks whether Becca brought the maple bar.
“She did.”
“Good.” At twenty past she gets up. Jack stays on his step with his back to the wall.

choices.text: Not tonight. Sit with her till she’s ready to go in.
response: Becca’s question can keep.

Lena talks about the fruitcake instead. It gets to Breaux Bridge on Friday, in the flat-rate box she wrote BE NOT AFRAID on in marker, and she would like to know whether the Breaux Bridge post office will take that as a threat, and whether Mémère will call to complain about the monks’ brandy or save it up to complain in person. Jack laughs where there’s room for it, and once where there isn’t, and she points at him for it. By the end she has the phone back in her lap with her hand over it, holding it shut.
At eight-thirty she stands and puts the phone in the cardigan pocket. “Goodnight, Jack.”

body: 412 is dark except for the ceiling. Jack is on his back under the blanket with his eyes open, and the room smells faintly of apple, which is the ficus.

Across the room Theo is a long shape under his duvet with his iPhone face up on his chest, and the screen throws a blue-white square onto the ceiling over his bed, over the water stain Jack has never mentioned to him. The overhead went off at midnight and nobody has said anything since. Down the hall, through two walls, Doug Pruitt is calling for a healer, louder and then louder, and then he stops.
On Jack’s desk the RAZR is shut, with the last thing it said still in it. He read it at a quarter to twelve, lying exactly like this.

And he does. The square on the ceiling brightens; his thumb taps once; the light goes out.

The screen on his chest stays lit a minute longer, and then it times out on its own.

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S → THE COURTYARD
body: At the 12:10 the blue glass turns noon into something underwater, and there are maybe fifteen people in a church built for three hundred: Mrs. Fitch in her pew by the shrine; an old man with a cane; two nursing students in scrubs; Joey Abruzzo in the second row, praying out loud by accident; Kenzie, who cantors the psalm like it costs her nothing; and in the fourth pew Becca, then Jack, then Lena. Osei says the Mass with his sleeves rolled under the vestments and preaches for two sentences.
Mrs. Fitch catches them in the vestibule after, by the holy water, in the lavender cardigan, and takes Becca by one arm and Jack by the other and squeezes. “*You two!*”

body.text: Becca told her yesterday afternoon, it turns out, when she stopped in to drop off the hospitality key and couldn’t keep it in. Mrs. Fitch has been pleased about it for twenty hours and isn’t close to done.
body.else: Becca goes scarlet. “I didn’t tell her!” “I saw you two on the Portolá steps from the 11 bus, dear,” says Mrs. Fitch. “Sharing a maple bar. I’m old, not blind.”

body.text: Lena is right there, holding the door for the old man with the cane. She lets it go when he’s through and turns around. “I’m happy for you, Jack.” Her hand goes to the medal. “I mean it.”
body.else: Lena holds the door for the old man with the cane and lets Mrs. Fitch have her moment.

body: Then Lena turns to Becca. “You’ll come to Sully’s Sunday? I’ll teach you the Who Dat.”
Becca lights up. “I’m making you a hotdish!”
“A what?”
“A *hotdish*. When somebody’s sad, everybody brings one, and then you have eleven.”

The courtyard at ten to one is olive shade and the broken sprinkler ticking in the planter, and Joey is under the tree with his flip phone held out at arm’s length. His father in Staten Island has been texting him. Joey reads it out at the volume he does everything at: a shooting at Fort Hood, the Army base in Texas, soldiers dead. “They keep changing the number,” he says. “It keeps going up.” Then his thumb stops on the keypad, and he holds the phone out for somebody else to read.

Osei comes out the side door with the stole still around his neck, gets it off Joey’s face before he gets it from Joey, and holds the door open behind him. “Come,” he says. “We’ll do this on our knees and read about it after.”

So they go back in, eight of them, and kneel in the front pew in the blue, and Kenzie starts the decade. Joey’s voice is too loud even when he whispers. The old man with the cane can’t kneel, so he stands at the end of the pew with one hand on the wood and says every word a half-beat behind everybody else. Jack gets through the first three Hail Marys on the words alone, and at the fourth he thinks of Yusuf’s brother, who interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls home on Sundays.

body: Nothing comes back for an hour. He checks at the bus shelter, and in line at the UCen, and on the steps of Hollis, and at 2:14, on the bench outside, it buzzes against his leg.

body.text: He’s not in Texas, Jack. He hasn’t called yet. He will. Talk tomorrow.

body: Jack puts the phone away and leaves the news alone.

Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. He hadn’t called yet.

body: The second-floor hall is loud with dinner — doors propped, somebody’s *Office* rerun, a microwave finishing somebody else’s popcorn — and Jack is carrying a Pyrex dish down the middle of it in a dish towel, at arm’s length, like something that could go off. It’s Becca’s mother’s Pyrex, which came down from Idaho in the Ranger in August against exactly this kind of emergency, LINDELL on a strip of masking tape across the lid, and the tater-tot hotdish inside is still warm through the towel from the Newman House oven. Becca walks beside him carrying the serving spoon. She knocks on 217 three times, briskly.
Laney opens the door in a green clay face mask and takes in the dish. “Is that a *casserole*?” she says. “Did somebody *die*?”
“Kind of!” says Becca.
Lena comes up behind Laney in her socks. She takes the dish from Jack in both hands, towel and all, and holds it against her. “Thank you, Becca.”
Jack, relieved of the dish, puts his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt.
“It’s better tomorrow,” Becca tells her. “Everything with cream of mushroom is.”

Laney is not finished. She explains to Becca, through the mask, that a hotdish at a time like this is a talent-portion violation — it is the baton-twirling of grief — and that Miss Congeniality is a fraud category, she has said so since she was nine years old; it’s the sash they give the girl who brought everybody a casserole.
“Lord have mercy,” says Lena. “Laney. Be nice.”
“This *is* my nice.”
Becca turns to Jack with her face lit. “She’s *funny*.”

And then, since nobody has told her this isn’t the moment, she starts in on the tots — you put them on top in rows, that’s the trick, rows, and you don’t crowd them or they steam — and Lena stands in the open doorway with the warm dish held against her and listens to every word, and Laney, green to the eyes, leans on the door and holds it wide.

s08.slug: FRIDAY · 6:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE CLIFF END — HALE’S HOUSE
body: Hale’s house smells of rib fat and Yorkshire-pudding smoke and the woodstove, and the smell comes out through the screen door and halfway down the walk to meet them. The last lot on the cliff end of Del Playa: a board-and-batten bungalow gone silver as driftwood, the canvas chair from Halloween empty on the porch, and past it only the dark and the sea working at the foot of the bluff.

Ten-point-two. It ran along the bottom of the Fishbowl TV this morning, between the Yankees and a commercial for a phone called Droid — UNEMPLOYMENT 10.2% IN OCTOBER, HIGHEST SINCE 1983 — and Jack stood there with his coffee and saw his father in the garage at home with the radio on and the door up to the cold, and didn’t call, and has been not calling all day.

Inside, books go to the ceiling on every wall that isn’t window. The woodstove ticks in the corner. On a Turkish rug worn to the threads Bishop Berkeley is asleep on his side, his long gray legs out in front of him like a card table somebody started to fold and gave up on. The dining table is a door — six panels, knob hole and all — laid across two trestles under a white cloth. Past it a glass slider opens onto a deck built out over the bluff, and past the deck is the Pacific, which at twenty to seven in November is only a darkness that breathes. Billie Holiday is on the turntable, low, and nobody remarks on her.

body.title: Propped against the candlestick, in Hale’s hand
body.text:
Standing rib of beef
Yorkshire puddings
Potatoes, roast, in the fat
Horseradish (real)
Sticky toffee pudding
—
Claret. Behave.

body: Hale is at the stove in shirtsleeves and an apron, basting, and doesn’t turn round. “Ten-point-two,” he tells the roasting pan. “I’ve cooked accordingly.” A dozen Yorkshire puddings are climbing out of a blackened tin in the oven, blistered and gold. “My mother’s tin,” he says, and shuts the oven on them.

The seminar arrives in a clump, early and apologizing. *Bring someone who’ll embarrass you.* The Palo Alto girl has brought a senior named Graham Fisk, in a Patagonia vest, who shakes Hale’s hand with both of his. The San Diego boys have brought each other. Caleb has come alone with a screw-top red he was specifically told not to bring; Hale puts it on top of the refrigerator, where it spends the night. Yusuf has a Tupperware of his mother’s dates and dark smudges under his eyes.
Becca is Jack’s, in the blue cardigan with the pearl buttons done up to the throat. She holds out the other jar of her mother’s huckleberry jam across the threshold, gingham and all.
“For the beef?” Hale says.
“For your *toast*. In the morning.” She looks at him with real concern. “You do eat breakfast.”
“Miss Lindell, I’m fifty-four. Breakfast is when I find out whether I’m alive.”
“Then it’s for that.”

Laney is Lena’s. She comes up the walk ahead of her in green silk and pearls with a bottle of Veuve Clicquot by the neck. “I said bring nothing,” says Hale. “This *is* nothing, sugar. It’s *Veuve*.” He takes the bottle and her elbow in one movement, and inside a minute the two of them are conspiring by the stove. Lena comes in last, in the cardigan over a dark green dress, and before she says good evening to anybody she crouches on the rug and lays her hand on the old dog’s ribs. Berkeley doesn’t wake. She waits out two of his breaths under her palm, then stands and says good evening to the room.
In the back bedroom, where the coats go on the bed, Becca asks it quietly, folding hers. “Do I embarrass you?”
“No.”
She nods and squeezes his arm and goes to tell Yusuf the dates look amazing.
Jack finds Yusuf a minute later by the shelves. “It’s tomorrow,” he says.
Yusuf almost smiles. “My brother called this morning. He’s fine. He said don’t watch the news.” He pushes a spine back into line with its neighbors. “I watched the news.”

They sit down to the door at half past seven. Hale carves standing, and pours the claret himself, down one side and up the other, into glasses held by people who can’t legally buy it. By this morning the major’s name and his religion are on every front page in the rack outside the UCen, and Graham Fisk has visibly been thinking about it all through the potatoes. He leans across the gravy, earnest, meaning it as a kindness. “Can I ask —” to Yusuf — “what do Muslims actually think about yesterday?”
“Mr. Noorzai is not a spokesman, Mr. Fisk,” Hale says, without raising his voice. “He’s a guest. Pass him the horseradish.”

Graham passes the horseradish. Yusuf measures out a careful spoonful. “I was going to say ‘the same as you,’” he tells Graham, “but the horseradish is better.” The table laughs, Graham hardest. Later, under the noise, Jack hears Yusuf say to the head of the table, “Thank you, Professor. I’d like one week where nobody asks,” and Hale raises his glass to him.

Becca crossed herself over her plate before she ate, small and quick, the way she does at every meal. Hale saw. He watches her eat with the attention he gives a paper he means to keep. “Miss Lindell believes in God without needing me to be wrong,” he announces. “It’s unbearable. Have more beef.” He puts another slice on her plate himself.
“Thank you! It’s *so* good. Is it Angus?”
“It’s from a man in Lompoc who swears at it.”
It’s a compliment, and it’s meant for her, and Jack, who has needed Hale to be wrong since he was sixteen, puts down his fork. The claret is at his elbow, nearly black in the candlelight.

choices.text: Hale’s claret, all evening.
response: It’s the best wine Jack has ever had, and he knows it inside one sip: dry and dark and faintly of cedar, the kind of thing he’s read about in novels and assumed was a lie. Hale fills him again without being asked, and again after that. Down the table Laney raises the Veuve at him in a toast she doesn’t explain.

choices.text: One glass, then water.
response: He makes the one glass last until the pudding, a sip at a time. When Hale comes round with the bottle Jack covers the rim with his hand, and Hale shrugs and fills Graham instead.

choices.text: Water.
response: He turns the wineglass upside down on the cloth.
“Abstemious, Mr. Costigan? On a *Friday*?”
“I’ve got a shift tomorrow.”
Hale is enchanted. “A temperance man at my table. How marvelous.” He fills Jack’s water glass himself, from a height, as a kind of insult.

Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks.

body: The sticky toffee pudding comes out in a dish the size of a hubcap, black at the edges and steaming, with a jug of cream. Yusuf considers it, and the ruins of the beef, and the potatoes left over. “I’ve been to eleven Catholic potlucks this year,” he says. “Not one of them ran out of food. It’s the only miracle I’ve personally verified.”

Hale taps his glass with a spoon. “You are in my house,” he says, “and therefore under my rule.” The rule from the second week: prove the thing you least believe you can prove. “The motion: whether a believer should go and say it to the world’s face, or come away. Mr. Costigan, who won in October by arguing for leaving and lost on Monday by arguing for nothing at all, will tonight argue for *going*. Miss Broussard, who has never left anything, will argue for the cave.” He sits back. “It counts. My table, my record.”
Chairs scrape round. Becca turns hers right around and folds her arms on the back of it.

Jack goes first, with the cream still going hand to hand. He gives them Paul in Athens: Acts seventeen, the city full of idols, an altar with an inscription — *To an unknown god* — and Paul standing up on the Areopagus in front of the cleverest men in Athens to say he’d come to introduce them. He didn’t quote the prophets at Athens. He quoted Athens at Athens, their own poet, *For we are indeed his offspring.* Then John seventeen, the night before, Christ praying over the eleven: *I do not pray that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from the evil one.* Not out. Kept, and in. The Church was a going before it was ever a building. “And you invited us, Professor,” he finishes, “and we came.”
Hale enjoys that a great deal more than he should.

Lena has her sleeves pushed to the elbow. “Benedict,” she says. “A rich boy from Norcia, sent to Rome to be educated, and he took one look at it and walked out. Gregory says he left *knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned*. Sat in a cave above a lake for three years while a monk let bread down to him on a rope.” She has no notes; she doesn’t need them. “And the West was kept alive by men who left it. MacIntyre ends the whole book there. *We are waiting not for a Godot, but for another — doubtless very different — St. Benedict.*” She looks down the length of the door at Jack. “He didn’t go to the barbarians, Costigan. He let Rome burn and copied the books.”

There’s a holy card of the other Benedict, the one in Rome now, in the back of the *Big Sur* on Jack’s desk. That man took the name for exactly this. He would take her side, Jack thinks, and hates it — and then he thinks of Regensburg, and isn’t sure.

choices.text: “Benedict left Rome. He didn’t leave the world. He built a better one in a cave, and the world walked up the hill to it.”
response: Lena pounces. “*Walked up the hill.* That’s my argument, Costigan. They came to *him*.”
It’s a clean exchange, and she gives him no ground at all, and he didn’t expect any.

choices.text: “Benedict went to a cave to get away from people and ended up running twelve monasteries. Some withdrawal.”
response: Twelve houses of twelve monks apiece; Gregory says so himself. The table goes up, Laney loudest, slapping the door so the glasses jump.
Lena waits it out. “And every one of them,” she says, “had a wall.”

choices.text: “He did. And the barbarians came to him.”
response: Hale tuts — actually tuts, like a housemaster — at generosity in his house.
Lena checks, half a beat, like she’s missed a step, and takes it, and goes on faster.

choices.text: “Your Benedict’s namesake went into Regensburg and argued faith and reason to the university’s face. And paid for it.”
response: September 2006: the old professor back at his old university, a lecture on *logos* to the faculty, and the world shouting about one quotation for a month after.

“And when Rome’s own university wouldn’t have him,” Lena says at once, “he didn’t go.” La Sapienza, January of last year: the faculty protested, the visit was cancelled, and he sent the speech anyway, and they read it out without him. “He came away, Costigan, and he left the door open. That’s *my* Benedict too.”
Hale looks from one of them to the other, delighted to have two popes at his table and believe in neither.

choices.text: “Going and staying aren’t opposites. Paul stayed in Corinth eighteen months. He made tents.”
response: Acts eighteen: a year and a half with Aquila and Priscilla, sewing tents between sermons, because a man has to eat.
“In *Corinth*,” Lena says. “Not on the moon.”
“*Tents!*” says Becca, and writes it on her napkin in ballpoint, and underlines it.

body: Her second move is the laugh in Athens.

“Acts seventeen, thirty-two,” Lena says. “*Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, ‘We will hear you again about this.’*” She folds her napkin in half on the cloth. “The politest no in Scripture. He goes to the smartest room in the world, quotes their own poets at them, and they say *bless your heart*. He never went back to Athens, Costigan. He went to Corinth and wrote them a letter about fools.”
First Corinthians: Christ crucified, a stumbling block and folly. Jack knows the letter. He wishes, briefly, that he didn’t.

body.text: “And Lucia,” she says, to him now and not the table. “We drove up a mountain in the fog for Vespers. Those monks didn’t come down the hill to anybody. We went up. We both heard them.”

body: Becca has been following every word from the back of her turned chair, working it like a sum. “She means you can’t make people come,” she says.
Lena turns to her across the cream jug, and for a second the table isn’t there. “That’s exactly what I mean.”

choices.text: “And Dionysius believed. And a woman named Damaris. You don’t go for the room. You go for the two.”
response: Acts seventeen, thirty-four: a judge of the Areopagus and a woman Luke never mentions again.
“Two,” Lena says. “Out of *Athens*.”
“Two’s how it starts. Ask the Twelve.”
She opens her mouth, and closes it, and comes at him from somewhere else.

choices.text: “Athens laughed. Athens hasn’t had a good century since.”
response: Hale objects at once, on behalf of Greece and of Oxford, which he appears to regard as the same country.
Lena doesn’t wait for him to finish. “Neither has Youngstown.”
The table laughs. Jack laughs a beat after it, because it’s true, and because of the Fishbowl TV this morning.

choices.text: “They laughed. He went anyway. That’s the part I can’t prove.”
response: Lena looks at him down the length of the door, and she isn’t arguing when she answers.
“No,” she says. “You can’t.”

choices.text: “You’d know. You never ask anybody the question you’re scared of.”
response: It wins the point. He knows where it lands while it’s still in the air — on September, on a question she let ride from Labor Day to All Souls because she is good at not noticing — and he feels it land before Hale has finished enjoying it.
Hale sits up, delighted. “*There* he is.”
Laney puts her fork down. Becca looks from face to face. “What? What’d I miss?”

Lena answers the argument. She answers it perfectly, level, every word of it to Hale. “Not asking isn’t the same as not knowing, Professor. Monica never argued Augustine into anything. She prayed for him for seventeen years and let Ambrose do the talking. Most of the praying in the world is done from a long way off.”

body: Her third move is quiet.

“Matthew ten,” Lena says. “He sends them out with no bag, no second tunic, and he tells them what to do when it doesn’t work. *And if any one will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet as you leave that house or town.*” She puts her fork down on the rim of her plate. “He *told* them to come away, Professor. It’s in the instructions.”
She says the rest lower, and not to Hale.
“Some people you can’t follow. You let them go, and you pray at a distance, and you leave the light on.”

Nobody at the table picks up a fork. In the corner the woodstove ticks. Becca waits politely for the next verse. Across the cream jug Laney has gone white under her freckles, and she is looking at Lena as if Lena had cut her hand on something and hadn’t noticed yet.

choices.text: “Leave the light on, then. You’re still going. Just slower.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you told Lena to leave the light on.
response: It doesn’t sound like anything. Graham reaches past the San Diego boys for the cream. Hale says, “Hm.”
Lena looks at Jack. Then she picks up her fork and goes back to her pudding.

choices.text: “The dust is for the town. Not for the people in it.”
response: “Tell that to the people in it,” Lena says.
“I’m telling *you*,” Jack says.
Somebody down the door says *oh*. Lena reaches for her water instead of the next verse, and takes her time with it.

choices.text: “Shaking off the dust was what you did leaving Gentile country. Look around, Miss Broussard. You’re at Hale’s.”
response: Hale roars. He slaps the door hard enough to slop the cream and claims Gentile country for his house in perpetuity, with Berkeley as its bishop.
Lena holds her hand out across the cloth to Jack, palm up. “Then pass the dust.”

choices.text: “What I said before. That was cheap, and it wasn’t an argument.”
response: “No,” Lena says. “It wasn’t.”
She doesn’t give him the point back.

body: Hale gives the floor ten minutes — Graham on the Crusades, briefly, unwisely; the chemistry kid, out of nowhere, on Thomas Merton; Caleb on nothing at all, his chair tipped back on two legs, watching Hale — and then he refills his own glass and gives his decision.

body.text: “Mr. Costigan has made Miss Broussard’s argument for her, at her expense,” Hale says. “The point goes where the cost is. Miss Broussard.” Five–three. “Thank you, Professor,” Lena says, to Hale, and to nobody else.

“An apology at my table, Mr. Costigan,” Hale says. “Retreat with honor is still retreat — which was her case. Miss Broussard.” Five–three. Lena inclines her head to the head of the table and touches her napkin to her mouth.
“Miss Broussard,” Hale says, “on the light. Mr. Costigan conceded the only point worth having. I didn’t know he could go that slowly.” Five–three.
“Mr. Costigan gave ground twice, and graciously,” Hale says, “which in a debate is called losing. Miss Broussard.” Five–three. Lena raises her glass to Jack, an inch, and doesn’t say what for.
Lena reaches for the cream jug, pours a little over what’s left of Jack’s pudding, and sets the jug back down by Graham.

“A draw,” Hale says. “Mr. Costigan was funnier than he was right, and Miss Broussard was more right than anyone needs to be at pudding.” Five–two, and one draw. Laney applauds alone, slowly, until the San Diego boys join in out of nerves.

“Mr. Costigan,” Hale says. “He went, and he came back with two. Miss Broussard was magnificent in defense of a cave.” Six–two. Lena lifts her glass an inch toward Jack. “Damaris,” she says, and drinks.
“Miss Broussard,” Hale says, “on points. She shook the dust off you in three moves.” Five–three. Jack eats his pudding. It’s very good pudding.

body: Hale pushes back from the door and goes to the kitchen for another bottle, and comes back with two.

body: The second bottle goes round, and round again. The record ran out somewhere during the duel and nobody has turned it over, so there’s only the woodstove and the sea under the deck and Hale’s voice, and the Yorkshire has started coming up through it, the vowels going short and flat. He has his jacket back on, the wine stain on the cuff gone purple in the candlelight, and his chair turned sideways to the door, one arm hooked over the back.

“I promised you marginalia over the pudding,” he says. “I keep my promises. It’s my one Christian quality.” And he begins to recite them, from memory, to the table, with attributions, intoning them like the lesson. “Mr. Costigan, on Miss Broussard, the first week: *This is the best paragraph I’ve read this year. I hate it.*”

body.text: Jack laughs. He’s three glasses in and it’s funny, and he’s still laughing when he sees that Lena isn’t.

body: “Also Mr. Costigan: *Coward.* Underlined. Miss Broussard, on Mr. Costigan: *Cite me.* And later, underlined once, in a hand like a ransom note: *Defense.*” He beams at the pair of them. “You see what I have to live with, darlings.”
Laney hoots. “Read *mine*, Professor.”
“You don’t write any, Miss Price.”
“I *would*.”
He takes two papers from inside his jacket, folded lengthwise, red all through. “This week’s.”

body.text: “Mr. Costigan, on Miss Broussard’s All Souls: *Monica asked to be remembered at the altar. So did Lucille. You did it.*” He lowers the page. “Sentiment. In red. Like a valentine from a dentist.”
“Mr. Costigan, on Miss Broussard’s All Souls: *You were owed. Consider it paid.*” He lowers the page. “A bookie’s margin.”
“Mr. Costigan, on Miss Broussard’s All Souls: *I argued Epicurus. I don’t believe a word of him. Neither did you.*” He lowers the page. “Honesty. In my seminar. I’ll have it framed.”

body: “I love that you guys look out for each other,” Becca says.

“And Miss Broussard, on Mr. Costigan.” Hale turns the second paper over, finds the corner folded down, and flattens it on the cloth with the side of his hand. “She’s dog-eared it, you’ll notice. A woman who folds down a margin wants it found.” He reads. “*You started another name on Monday and stopped. Whoever it is —*”
Hale stops.
He looks at the page. “Ah,” he says. He folds it in half, and in half again, and puts it away inside his jacket, and picks up his glass.
“What’s the rest?” Becca asks.
“Illegible,” says Hale.
Down the door Lena is looking at the place on Hale’s jacket where the paper went. Jack looks at his plate.

“Instead,” Hale says, brightly, to the room. “Two people at this table wrote to me before they ever sat in my seminar. At length. To a stranger. To tell him he was wrong about God. I answered them both. A postcard each — same card, same line.” He drinks. “I buy them at Blackwell’s by the hundred. I’ve used three.” He smiles down the table. “Mr. Costigan’s nine pages, from Ohio. Miss Broussard’s twelve, from New Orleans. Longer. She always is.”
Jack turns and looks at her. Twelve pages, from New Orleans. Ten weeks across an oak table from him, a postcard the whole time, and she never said.
Lena hasn’t moved. Her hand has gone to the medal at her throat, and it holds there.
Caleb’s chair comes down onto all four legs. “You wrote back to *her*?”
Hale doesn’t answer. Caleb looks at him with his face wide open. “I wrote you four letters.”
“I know,” Hale says. “I keep them.” He looks into his glass. “I don’t answer devotion, Mr. Hargrove. It doesn’t need me.”
Caleb sits with that for the space of one breath. Then he folds his napkin, sets it square on his plate, gets up, and goes out the front, past the bedroom with the coats on the bed, without his.
“Bloody boy,” Hale tells his glass, the vowel gone short and northern, pure Barnsley, and drinks.

A minute later Lena gets up too. She says something low to Laney that Jack doesn’t catch and goes out through the slider onto the deck, and Berkeley climbs up off the rug joint by joint and follows her out into the dark.
Becca leans into Jack’s shoulder. “Is he always like this?” she says, very quietly.
Laney sets her glass down and doesn’t pick it up again. At the head of the door Hale is pouring.

journal.title: The postcard
journal.text: She read the back of my postcard twice. Asked who A.H. was like she didn’t care. She cared. Hale’s table: he buys them at Blackwell’s by the hundred and has used three. Mine was nine pages. Lena wrote him twelve. She has one too.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion.

s13a.slug: FRIDAY · 9:38 PM · SHIPWRECK COVE, THE STAIRS
body: The stairs down to Shipwreck Cove start where Del Playa runs out of pavement: a switchback of gray two-by-fours bolted into the bluff, with a string of Christmas lights stapled along the rail that nobody has plugged in for years. The moon is up behind the houses now and the bluff throws its shadow down the flight, so Jack goes down by the rail and by memory, with Caleb’s coat over his arm — Goodwill corduroy, too big in the shoulders, a library receipt in one pocket.

Caleb is on the second landing in his shirtsleeves with his knees up. He doesn’t turn when the boards announce somebody coming. Jack holds out the coat, and after a second Caleb takes it and keeps it in his lap.

“The first one was just *thank you*,” Caleb says. Visalia is all through his vowels; he sounds about twelve. “Eleven pages of thank you. The second one was questions. Real ones — I had footnotes. The third one was about my dad’s church.” He works at a splinter in the step with his thumbnail. “What happened to it. I never wrote that down for anybody. I figured he’s the one guy, you know? He’d get it.” The splinter comes up. “The fourth one I just asked if he got the third one.”
Below them the cove is black. The fire ring is cold, and the tide is in over the old schooner’s ribs.
“Did *she* know?” Caleb says. “That you both —”
“I didn’t.”
Caleb laughs through his nose. “Dude. You’ve sat next to her for ten weeks.”
“Across from her.”
“Across from her.” He looks at the coat. “My dad never answered either,” he says. “He just *smiled*.”
Jack doesn’t try to fix it. He sits down on the step above, close enough that their shoulders would touch if either of them leaned, and they look at the water.
Eventually Caleb stands up and puts the coat on. It takes him two tries to find the second sleeve.
“That’s enough, Professor.”
The table stops. Graham’s fork halts halfway to his mouth. One of the San Diego boys sets his glass down on the door without a sound.

Hale looks at Jack across the candles and the wreck of the pudding, and keeps looking, until the San Diego boy picks his glass back up just to have something to hold. The color is high in Hale’s face. His eyes are perfectly steady.
“Yes,” he says. “It is.”
And he pours himself another anyway, to the rim, and drinks a third of it, and sets it down. Then, the way he’d tell a man his shoelace was undone: “You’ll do, Mr. Costigan.”

That breaks it. The San Diego boys discover an early something and go to find their coats on the bed. Graham finds his date’s and holds it open for her. Under the cloth Becca’s hand finds Jack’s knee and squeezes, once.
Beside Jack, Yusuf murmurs, “Factor of safety,” and starts stacking plates. Across the door Laney puts her chin in her hand and looks at Jack properly, for the first time all fall.

Caleb’s corduroy is still on the bed, under everybody else’s. Through the slider, past his own reflection in the glass, Jack can see Lena out on the deck at the rail, and the long gray shape of the dog at her feet.

The deck is ten degrees colder than the house. The moon has cleared the roof behind them, and the bungalow’s shadow falls out over the boards and across the rail and stops in the air above the drop. Below, the water that was black at seven is going gray from the horizon in.
Lena is on the bench at the rail with her back to the north-west and Berkeley’s long head in her lap. Her cardigan is pulled tight, and one hand is working on the dog’s ear, back and back.
“I’m fine.”
“I know.”

He sits at the other end of the bench. Berkeley shifts with a groan and stretches out between them, his spine against Jack’s leg and his head where it was — deaf, and asleep again before Jack has settled.
“He’s the only one at this party with any sense,” Lena says.

Behind them, through the glass, the dinner goes on without sound: Hale talking with his hands; Laney with her chin propped, watching him; Becca on her feet, stacking plates, because there are dirty dishes on a table. A gull goes over in the dark, low, white for a second where the light from the slider catches it.
Jack puts his hand on the dog’s ribs, near his own end. Berkeley breathes under it. Lena’s hand keeps on with the ear. They let the old dog sleep.

At quarter to eleven Becca stands up from a stack of rinsed plates and announces the tank: the swine-flu volunteer is still out, it’s six in the morning again, and Thomas’s neighbors are not going to feed themselves. Laney, who has been lying full length on Hale’s rug, holds up one arm without opening her eyes.
“I’m *exhausted*, farmer. Drive me.”
“Okay! Do you get carsick?”
“I get *everything*.”

body.text: Caleb comes up the walk out of the dark with his coat buttoned to the neck. “Oh, good, you’re *alive*,” Becca says, and he folds himself into the middle of the Ranger’s bench seat with his knees up around his ears, Laney on one side of him and Becca on the other.

Becca has Caleb’s corduroy over her arm, out of the back bedroom. “It’s *November*,” she tells the street. “We’ll find him. He’s walking, he can’t have got far.” She lays it folded on the Ranger’s bench seat between herself and Laney, like a passenger.

body: Becca stops at the Ranger’s open door with the keys on their carabiner in her fist. “Walk Lena home?” she says. “She shouldn’t walk by herself.” She goes up on her toes and kisses his cheek, and gets in, and the truck’s headlights swing across Hale’s hedge and go away up Del Playa.

Hale is in the doorway with the light behind him and a glass in his hand, swaying a little, a big man filling a small frame. Lena has come round from the deck and is on the step below Jack, doing up the buttons of her cardigan. Hale looks down at the pair of them for some time.
“I wrote to you both,” he says, “because you were the only ones who wrote *at* me like you meant it.”

body.text: His eyes come to Jack. “Even you. *Especially*.”

body: Then he looks past them, west, toward the Point and its dead light.

s15.slug: FRIDAY · 10:50 PM · DEL PLAYA → SEACLIFF → THE GROVE
body: The night has gone cool and dead still, upper fifties and not a breath off the water, and the moon is well up over the mountains now, four nights past full and lopsided with it, bright enough to throw the shadows of the Del Playa mailboxes across the street. Below the bluff the sea is lit all the way out, with nothing on it. *Walk Lena home*, Becca said, and so he is.

body.text: She is perfectly courteous to him the length of Del Playa. She asks whether he has his key; she says *Jack* every time she needs a name; it is all one degree colder than it was at seven, and she walks beside him anyway.
Hale’s claret is still in his knees, and at the second driveway Lena takes a fistful of his sleeve and steers him back onto the sidewalk. “You’re tilting.” “Ships list.” “Ships have keels.”
body.else: His head is clear, and so is the cold: the smell of somebody’s woodsmoke, the jasmine on a fence, her boots on the concrete beside his Chucks.

body: On Seacliff he moves to the street side of the sidewalk without thinking about it, the way his father taught him on Glenwood Avenue. Two blocks on she notices which side of him the street is on.
“You’re being very careful with me, Costigan.”
They walk.

Under the last streetlight before the Grove she takes her wallet out of the cardigan, slides something from behind her driver’s license, and holds it out to him while she looks up the road. A postcard, carried so long it has gone soft as cloth, the corners rounded off. He knows it before it’s in his hand.
“I asked you who A.H. was,” she says.
“You read it twice.”
“I read it *once*.” Now she looks at him. “Then I read mine, in my head.”
He thinks of the porch on the first night, and how easily she gave his back.
“Twelve pages,” he says.

“Spring of ’08.” They go on into the trees. “Two years after the year I went to Mass every morning to yell at Him. Somewhere in that year it stopped being a fight, and I’d been furious about that ever since. I wanted somebody to tell me I was right to be angry, and the only man I could find who’d argue with me properly didn’t believe in Him either.” She takes the card back. “Your turn. Nine pages. From Ohio.”

body.text: So he tells her about the summer he was sixteen, when he read Hale’s book in three nights and quit going. Every Sunday that summer he drove his mother to St. Brigid’s in the Silverado and sat in the lot with the radio off while she went in, and she never once asked him to come, and some Sundays he sat there with the engine off, willing her to. “Something happened that fall,” he says. “I started again.” Lena waits, in case there’s more. There isn’t, and she doesn’t ask.
body.else: “I was seventeen,” he says. “I’d read him at sixteen and thought I’d found a hole.” “Did you?” “He wrote back,” Jack says. “That’s a hole.” And she laughs, a little.

body: In the Grove the moon comes down through the trees in pieces, and she talks about Wes without saying his name, and then not about Wes at all. “It isn’t only him,” she says. “There’s a house on Zimple Street, two doors from his. A shotgun with a fig tree in the side yard and a For Sale sign up since the storm. I had my grandmother’s sewing table in the front window. In my head.” She puts the card back behind her license. “I’d picked the *paint*, Jack. Haint blue for the porch ceiling, so the wasps think it’s sky.” She goes on, in order: their babies baptized at Holy Rosary in the family gown; Mémère’s ring on her own hand at last; Sunday dinners on Dupre Street with Wes and Luc arguing about the Corps over the gumbo. Jack hears every room.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. I tried to argue her out of something. She’s not a case.

journal.title: Not a case
journal.text: Walking down from Hale’s, I tried to argue Lena out of blaming herself. ‘Don’t argue me out of it, Costigan. I’m not a case.’ She was right.

The front room: the sewing table in the window, the Singer her grandmother pedaled in her stocking feet. He asks which wall the books go on. “All of them.” The bedroom she skips, fast, and he lets her. He asks where the dog sleeps. “What dog?” “There’s always a dog.” “Under the kitchen table,” she decides. “Boudreaux.” Then the bathroom, where the claw-foot tub won’t fit — she measured the listing photos with a ruler — so the tub goes out on the back porch under the fig, and she hears herself say it and laughs up into the trees.
“Curtain?” Jack says. “Or just the fig?”
“Just the fig. It’s *Uptown*. They’ve seen worse.” She wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand, and it isn’t only from laughing.

She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch.

response: He walks beside her and says nothing.

Where the path dips toward the creek the trees close over and the moon quits, and in the dark she puts her hand through the crook of his arm and holds on, her weight on it wherever the path goes uneven.
He keeps his arm where she put it. He doesn’t reach for her hand. They come out of the trees that way into the Anacapa lights, and she lets go to fix her hair.

s16.slug: SATURDAY · 12:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK
body: At twenty to one Delgado’s lobby is the hum of the Coke machine and a night clerk, a sophomore with a chemistry text under the desk lamp, who never looks up. Lena leans on the front desk. Jack takes the stairs.

body.text: 412 is dark. The silk robe is over Theo’s chair. Jack finds the card by feel in his desk drawer, where it has lived since *The Moviegoer* went to Theo.
body.else: 412 is dark. The silk robe is over Theo’s chair. Jack slides the card by feel out of *The Moviegoer* on his desk, where it has been the bookmark since August.

body: On the stairs back down his RAZR shows a text from twenty past eleven.

body.text: she sang hymns the WHOLE way. i know all the words to be not afraid now. i hate it here

body: Downstairs she has hers out on the desk already. He lays his beside it under the lamp, picture side up.

The Radcliffe Camera, both of them: the round library at Oxford, its ring of paired columns and its lead dome, the stone the color of toast in a printed sun, the sky behind it a blue nobody in England has seen since the war. Along the bottom edge, in type small enough to need the lamp, BLACKWELL’S · OXFORD. They turn them over together. On the back of each, in fountain pen, black ink gone faintly brown, the same line in the same tall, backward-leaning hand: *Come and say it to my face. —A.H.* The A and the H run into each other. His is addressed to Glenwood Avenue, Youngstown; hers to North Dupre Street, New Orleans. Both are postmarked MARISOL CA, 2008, hers in March and his in June, and the stamps are a cent apart — twenty-six for hers, twenty-seven for his, after the rate went up in May. Hers is worn round at the corners. His has a brown half-ring in one corner where his mother set a cup of Folgers down on it, the morning it came.
“Same pen,” Jack says.
“Same *line*.” She squares the cards with the edge of the desk. “He didn’t even change the dash.”

choices.text: “Trade me. Till Sunday.”
response: She slides his card toward herself and fits it behind her license, coffee ring and all. Hers goes in his shirt pocket, to go up into *Big Sur*.
“Goodnight, Jack,” she says at the foot of the stairs.

choices.text: Slide hers back. Each keeps their own.
response: He slides hers back with one finger. She puts it where it lives and snaps the wallet shut. “Good,” she says, and seems to mean more than one thing by it.
“Goodnight, Jack,” she says at the foot of the stairs.

choices.text: “Keep both tonight. Yours could use the company.”
response: She laughs, and takes them both, his on top of hers, and puts the pair away behind her license together.
“Goodnight, Jack,” she says at the foot of the stairs.

s17.slug: SATURDAY · 7:12 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE KITCHEN OFF THE FISHBOWL
body: The sun comes through the Fishbowl glass low enough to lay a bar of gold down the kitchen counter, across the Mr. Coffee and the Newman stockpot with its dent to the wall. Lena has her hands in the pot to the wrists, picking chickens for tomorrow’s soup, her hair up in a gumband. Jack came down for coffee.
On the counter by the salt, her LG goes off.
“That’s Mémère.” She points at it with her chin. “Speaker. Push the — yes.”

“*Magdalena?*” A small, ferocious voice, pitched for long distance and a deaf parish. It is 9:12 in Breaux Bridge, Mémère is home from the eight o’clock at St. Bernard’s, and she reports in French without a pause for breath. Lena translates over her shoulder, or some of it. The fruitcake came Friday. It is *trop sec* — too dry — and she is eating it anyway, a slice every morning cut thin enough to read the *Teche News* through. She lit a candle for Wesley at the eight o’clock. “*C’est un bon garçon,*” the phone says, sharp. “*Le Bon Dieu a pas fini avec lui.*”
“He’s a good boy,” Lena says to the chicken. “God’s not finished with him.”
Then something lower and fast, and the end of it Jack catches himself, with two years of Cardinal Mooney French and no help from anybody: *Quelqu’un devait demander.*
Lena doesn’t translate that one. Her hands stop in the pot and then go on.

Somebody had to ask. Jack thinks he knows what. He has carried it since a picture on Wes’s phone at three in the morning on Columbus Day weekend: this woman’s ring, a small high stone on a band her own hand wore thin, waiting in a desk drawer on Zimple Street; and since the stairs, the old woman at the tomb on All Saints with a dripping brush, asking when. He drinks his coffee and keeps all of it where it has been all week.
He sets the cup down on the counter, and Mémère hears it. A torrent. Lena closes her eyes. “She wants to know who is in my kitchen at seven o’clock in the morning.”
“Tell her it’s a communal kitchen.”
“I’m not telling her *communal*. She’ll think it’s a commune.” Then, to the phone: “*C’est Jack, Mémère.* From down the hall. He came for coffee.”
The torrent stops dead. Then: “*Ah. Et le garçon de l’Ohio?*” And in English, slow and clear, aimed straight across the counter at him like a finger: “Wesley said you’re skinny.”

choices.text: “Oui, madame.”

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners.

response: “*Oui, madame,*” he says, to the phone, with the little bow his nonna would expect.

There’s a pause in Breaux Bridge while this is weighed. “*Bon,*” Mémère decides. “He has manners. Feed him, Magdalena.” And then a good deal more in French that Lena translates as “She says goodbye.” It is plainly not all of it.

choices.text: Tell her the truth about the Browns.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. She pities me for the Browns. Lena says that’s the highest honor they have.

response: “I’m a Browns fan, ma’am,” he tells the phone. “We’re one and seven. We’ve got a bye this week. It’s our best matchup of the year. They fired the general manager on Monday.”
Lena translates. Breaux Bridge takes it in. Then, with real feeling: “*Pauvre garçon.*”
“She pities you,” Lena says, and the corner of her mouth has come up. “That’s the highest honor we have.”
