journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I told her in French that I’m skinny. She laughed at me for a full minute.

response: He leans over the phone and reaches back to Mrs. Kovach and the language lab. “*Je suis…* ” The word arrives. “*…maigre?*”

Mémère cackles, a high, eighty-eight-year-old noise that goes on and on, broken by coughing and by French he’s sure he shouldn’t repeat to his mother. At the pot Lena’s shoulders are going, her wet hands held up out of the way, until she has to turn to the window.

s17a.slug: SATURDAY · 7:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE KITCHEN OFF THE FISHBOWL
body: When the call is over she lifts her hands out of the pot and holds them up, dripping, like a surgeon’s, and goes and stands at the Fishbowl window. Outside the Anacapa lawn is wet and shining, and a girl in pajama pants is dragging a bag of laundry across it by the drawstring.
“I need to not be in this building today,” Lena says.
“Okay,” says Jack.
She turns around. She looks at him over her held-up hands, and then she nods, once. “You pick,” she says. “I’ll go.”

choices.text: “The Old Mission. It’s Saturday — somebody’ll be getting married.”
choices.key: The Saturday after Hale’s dinner you took Lena to the Old Mission, and you sat at the back of a stranger’s wedding.

choices.text: “The harbor. You can yell at a man about rockfish.”
choices.key: The Saturday after Hale’s dinner you took Lena to the harbor fish market, and she bought a rockfish for the night shift.

s18a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:00 AM · OLD MISSION NUESTRA SEÑORA DEL MAR
s18a.music: A wedding mariachi — “El Son de la Negra”
body: Trumpets, first, from a block away: a mariachi on the Old Mission steps in black and silver, nine men in charro suits with the sun all over their buttons, playing the guests up out of the parking lot like a brass band at a ballgame. An old man in a straw hat stands at the bottom with his eyes shut, conducting with one finger. Lena stops dead on the sidewalk.
“Oh,” she says. “Oh, they *came*.”

They go in behind an aunt in purple and sit in the last pew, under the choir loft, like people who were invited. The adobe keeps the cold of two hundred years in it, and the light comes down sideways from deep windows onto walls painted with vines. Somebody has left a program in their pew.

body.title: A program, left in the back pew
body.text:
Yesenia Montoya & Rubén Salazar
7 de noviembre de 2009
Misa de Matrimonio

body: The ring bearer is four, in a tiny tuxedo, and halfway up the aisle he stops, considers the satin pillow, and starts eating the fringe off it. The mother of the groom half rises in the second pew. Lena laughs out loud, in church, and doesn’t care who hears, and Jack catches it off her and has to look up at the ceiling beams. The boy gets the rings to the front with the fringe in his teeth.

The vows come in Spanish and English both, and then the rings. After the rings, the arras: thirteen gold coins, blessed, poured from Rubén’s cupped hands into Yesenia’s, chiming, and not one dropped. Up in the loft the mariachi has moved inside, and the trumpets have gone soft and slow for something Jack doesn’t know.

Later, before the blessing, the padrinos come forward with the lazo, a long loop of white cord strung with beads like a rosary, and lay it in a figure eight over the bride’s shoulders and the groom’s, so that the two of them kneel there joined, one cord around both. Yesenia bows her head under it.

Lena cries at the lazo. She doesn’t make any noise doing it. She just sits very straight in the last pew of a stranger’s wedding with the tears coming, looking at the two people under the one cord. Jack doesn’t say anything wise. He goes into the Carhartt and finds a napkin from the Anchor, folded in four, the anchor printed in blue in its corner, and hands it to her. She takes it and uses it and keeps it.
“In New Orleans,” she says thickly, “we’d have a second line out the door.”

They slip out at the Lamb of God, before the Communion line, so nobody has to count them. On the bright steps Lena puts her sunglasses on and stands with the napkin balled in her fist, listening to the trumpets come out through the doors behind them.

s18b.slug: SATURDAY · 10:30 AM · THE HARBOR, THE FISH MARKET
body: Sea lions have the float at the end of the wharf, eleven of them heaped together, wet and enormous, and one big bull is up on his flippers barking at the boats like a tuba with a cold. The Anchor is down the boards with its OPEN sign lit in the daylight. The fish market is a cinderblock shed with its roll-up door open on long steel trays of ice.

Lena goes down the trays slowly, hands behind her back, the way Jack’s nonna goes down a church bazaar. She stops at a rockfish, a big red one with its mouth open in permanent outrage, and leans over and looks it straight in the eye.
“Daddy taught me,” she says. “Clear eyes, red gills, and it shouldn’t smell like anything but the sea. If it smells like *fish*, it’s too late for both of you.”

The fishmonger is a broad man in a rubber apron and a backward Raiders cap, and he has clearly been waiting all week for somebody like her. She asks what he wants for it, and when he tells her, she tells him, in Banks Street English and with gestures, what that rockfish is worth, who it was in life, and what it would bring at her father’s counter on a bad Friday in Lent. “Oh, Magdalena is *not* paying that,” she tells Jack, “for a fish that looked at her like that.” He comes down a dollar a pound and throws in the heads. “Lagniappe,” Lena tells him, and he says it back wrong, and she lets him.
She buys it for the night shift: a court-bouillon on Monday, because Dulce and Rosario have had chicken every Sunday since September.

While he wraps it she tells Jack about the summer after the storm, when Broussard’s Seafood opened back up and Wes came to work the counter at seventeen. He was hopeless at filleting. He left half the fish on the bones, and her father stood at the register pretending not to watch, so the boy wouldn’t quit. She says the name like any other.
The fishmonger hands the fish across the ice in its newspaper. Jack takes it, because he’s closer.
“Daddy says you can tell a man by how he holds a fish,” Lena says.
Jack looks down. He is holding it like a loaf of bread, or a baby, or a rolled-up rug; he can’t tell which, and none of them is right. The tail is drooping out of the paper toward his shoe.
Lena takes it from him and tucks it against her hip, and she carries it herself back up the wharf, past the sea lions, and doesn’t give it back.

s19.slug: SATURDAY · 3:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: Afternoon comes through the blue glass and fills the overturned hull of the church like water. The confession line runs down the side aisle past the Marian shrine, where the Book of the Dead lies shut on its stand. A Saturday line: two nursing students, a grad student with a bike helmet hooked on his elbow, and Joey Abruzzo directly in front of them, explaining in what he believes is a whisper that he examines his conscience off a laminated card from his grandmother and it has never let him down.
The converted coat closet opens and closes. Joey goes in and comes out four minutes later looking freshly hosed down.

Then Lena. She goes in and the door shuts on her, and Jack sits down on the kneeler of the nearest pew, and doesn’t time her, and it’s eleven minutes. He hears nothing; somebody padded that door with carpet in 1962 for exactly this. He looks at the driftwood crucifix and says a decade without deciding what for, and halfway through it he is praying for the woman on the other side of the carpet, and goes on.
When she comes out she walks past the line with her hands in her cardigan pockets and her face washed clean, and sits down at the end of the back pew, and bows her head.

choices.text: Go in after her.
choices.key: Saturday at 3:30 you went to confession after Lena.
response: He takes the chair, not the kneeler, and says what he came to say. It takes less time than he thought and costs more.

Fr. Osei is quiet on the other side of the screen. When the voice comes it is low, amused at something that isn’t Jack: “Your penance is to let somebody help you this week.” The words of absolution. The sign of the cross through the grille.
When he comes out, Lena is still in the back pew. She looks up, sees where he has been, and moves her purse over to make room.

choices.text: Don’t. You’re here for her.
response: He gets up off the kneeler and goes and sits in the back pew, at the other end from her, and lets the grad student have his turn.
When Lena lifts her head she looks at the line, where he isn’t, and then down the pew at him, where he is. She moves her purse to her other side, out of the way, and puts her head back down.

s20.slug: SATURDAY · 5:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE VIGIL
body: Becca has saved three seats in the fourth pew with her clipboard, her cardigan and her purse, and waves them in from the aisle like ground crew. Becca, Jack, Lena. Gus is into the prelude, and the five o’clock fills up behind them.

body.text: Jack is still light from the box. When the entrance hymn goes up he sings it, out loud, the whole first verse.

body: Peter Haddad reads Kings in his long robe of a voice: the widow of Zarephath, the last handful of flour, the prophet asking her for bread anyway. *Do not be afraid.* Kenzie cantors the psalm. Osei reads Mark — the scribes who like long robes and the best seats, the widow and her two small coins — and preaches hardly at all. He ends: “Jesus does not say she was sensible. He says she gave more than all of them.”
At the Our Father Becca takes his hand. Her palm is warm and rough, a working hand, and she holds on. On his other side Lena’s hands stay folded.

On the way out Mrs. Fitch is on the top step in the lavender cardigan with the second collection, for the St. Vincent de Paul pantry, taken at the doors: a long-handled wicker basket she holds out to each person like a fishing net. It reaches Becca first. She puts in a folded bill, and the basket comes to Jack.

choices.text: This week’s tips. All of them.
response: The week’s tips are in an envelope in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, ANCHOR across the flap in Gloria’s grease pencil. He puts the whole envelope in the basket. Becca sees, and squeezes his arm hard enough to hurt.
Then she’s off to the early bed and the six o’clock tank. “Lena, go to the Anchor with him!” she calls from the sidewalk. “Gloria will feed you!”

choices.text: A five.
response: He puts in a five, and Mrs. Fitch moves the basket on to Lena.
Then Becca’s off to the early bed and the six o’clock tank. “Lena, go to the Anchor with him!” she calls from the sidewalk. “Gloria will feed you!”

choices.text: Everything in his pocket, bus fare included.
response: He empties his jeans into the basket: two ones, a five, the quarters for the 11, a Canadian dime somebody passed him at the Anchor, and the receipt from the Driftwood cart. He fishes the receipt back out.
Lena has watched all of it. “Now you’re walking home,” she says, low.
“I was always walking home.”
Then Becca’s off to the early bed and the six o’clock tank. “Lena, go to the Anchor with him!” she calls from the sidewalk. “Gloria will feed you!”

body: Rudy’s transistor is on the shelf over the fryer, tuned to KNX, and the House of Representatives comes through it between the hiss of the baskets and the Hobart’s long gargle, men from Ohio and Michigan yielding to each other at the tops of their voices. Rudy listens the way he listens to Vin Scully, without once looking up from the flat-top.

body.text: Lena paid both fares on the 11, and La Flaca rode the rack on the front of the bus, and the driver said nothing about the girl or the bike, which Jack took as grace.

body: Lena is on the counter stool nearest the dish station, where he can see her through the pass, with Hale’s packet for Monday and a pencil and a slice of buttermilk pie she didn’t order; Gloria took one look at her and decided.

body.text: The rockfish is in Rudy’s walk-in under a sign in her capitals: LENA’S. MONDAY. FOR THE HARBOR INN. TOUCH IT AND I’LL KNOW.

body: A little after eight the radio man has it. The Stupak amendment went through earlier in the evening, two hundred forty to one ninety-four, while they were at the vigil; now the bill itself passes, two-twenty to two-fifteen, and the only Republican to vote yes, the radio says, was Joseph Cao, of Louisiana’s Second District — New Orleans. Through the pass Jack sees Lena put down her pencil.
“That’s my city,” she tells Rudy. “That’s *New Orleans*.” Rudy lifts his spatula to her, gravely, and goes back to the flat-top.
At half past eight Gloria is at the pass, counting the tip jar into stacks of quarters. She doesn’t look up from them, and she has seen who is on the end stool.
“So this is waiting,” she says.
Then she sweeps the stacks into an envelope and goes off with it. At nine she takes his apron.
On the stool beside her he gets the speech.

“Charity’s been shut since the storm, Jack. Four years. The biggest hospital for poor people in Louisiana, and it’s got plywood on the windows.” She taps the pencil on Hale’s packet. “Daddy’s shrimpers haven’t had insurance since they’ve had boats. And my congressman — a Vietnamese man from New Orleans East who was a Jesuit before he was a lawyer — voted for them tonight, because they kept every dollar of it off abortion. Both, Jack. In one bill. I didn’t think I’d live to see both.”
“I came for the amendment,” Jack says. “The doctors are your department.”
“Everything’s my department,” Lena says, with her mouth full of pie.

Gloria keeps the coffee coming and charges them for none of it. The LG lights up on the counter, and Lena reads it and turns it face down. “Remy. LSU lost in Tuscaloosa. He’ll be in mourning till Easter.” Then Jack’s RAZR goes off in his jeans, and it seems Ohio State has won at Penn State.

body.text: PRYOR!!!

body: At ten the LG rings. Lena looks at it. “It’s Margot,” she says, and picks up, and holds the phone a little away from her ear, so Jack can hear it too.

Margot is furious. She makes her best argument, and it’s a good one: the amendment bars any plan bought with a subsidy on the new exchange from covering abortion, no insurer will write two kinds of policy for one market, so women who *have* that coverage now, in private plans, will lose it. “And the answer is a *rider*,” she says. “Nobody buys a rider for an unplanned pregnancy, Lena. That’s what *unplanned* means.”
Lena puts the phone down on the counter between the pie and the sugar and looks at it.
“She may be right about the private plans,” she says to Jack. “She’s wrong about the baby.”

choices.text: Take Lena’s side against Margot.
response: He leans to the phone and tells Margot that a child isn’t a line item, and he’ll say so in front of her whiteboard any day she likes. Margot hangs up in the middle of a subordinate clause.
Lena looks at him over the pie. “Same side,” she says. “Write it down. Margot’s going to want it for the board.” And she slides him the rest of the pie.

choices.text: Give Margot her point too.
response: “She might be right about the private plans,” Jack says. “Nobody knows yet. Somebody could lose something they had.”
“Traitor,” Lena says fondly, and puts Margot on speaker.
Margot’s voice comes up off the Formica, tinny and precise. “Is that Costigan? Tell Costigan he’s on the board.”
“She means it nicely,” Lena tells him.
“I do not,” says the phone.

choices.text: “Cao. One Republican, and he’s yours.”
response: “One Republican in the House of Representatives,” Jack says, “and he’s yours.”
“He’s *mine*,” Lena says, and lifts her coffee cup to the radio. “The only one.” She picks up the phone. “Margot. Margot, I have to go. I have a congressman.”

s22.slug: SUNDAY · 12:55 AM · MISSION STREET → OCEAN ROAD → THE GROVE
body: The last 11 left at half past twelve while they were still at the counter, so they walk it, three miles, Jack pushing La Flaca and Lena on the other side of the bike with her hand on the basket. The moon came up late and is over the mountains now, small and very white. The Borders is dark. The Blockbuster is dark, and looks it.

body.text: Tonight he lets her finish every sentence she starts.

body: Somewhere past Giorgio’s she starts on Thanksgiving. Wes will be at the table on Dupre Street. He has been at every Broussard Thanksgiving since 2005; he is Luc’s best friend, and he has a chair.
“He carried the twins out of a second floor, Jack,” she says. “Mama’s not going to *not* set him a place.”
“The twins.”

“Jude and Josie. They were nine. The water was up to the gutters on the neighbors’ house, and he put them in the boat one at a time through the window, and Josie bit him.” She almost smiles. “She’s thirteen now. She still brags about it.” Then: “And I’ll be at the kids’ end with Josie, passing him the rolls.”

Where Ocean Road tips down toward campus she says, “Stop,” and gets up sidesaddle on the little rack over La Flaca’s back fender. He walks the bike down the grade with her on it, then lets it roll, then has to run, her laughing behind him with her boots held up off the asphalt, down to the flat by the dark Commons, where the second floor of the Brick is lit all night.
At the bottom she stays where she is on the rack, and he walks on, slower, pushing the both of them.
“I’d go anywhere on the twenty-sixth,” she says. “Anywhere nobody knows his name.” And in the same breath, lightly, to the back of his head: “Is Becca going home with you? To Youngstown?”
“She’s going home to Idaho. Her mom named the turkey.”
“Right,” Lena says. “Of course she is.”

*Then come to Youngstown* is right there in his mouth, all of it, ready. He can hear how it would land: one breath after Becca’s name — *she can’t, so you* — and five days after Wes, the extra chair at the table, offered to whoever’s standing nearest. Not like that. A week from now he’ll ask her properly, when it’s an invitation and not a consolation prize.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name.

choices.text: “Come where nobody knows his name.”
choices.key: Walking home at one in the morning, Lena said she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. You took her to Lupe’s.
response: “Come where nobody knows his name,” he says, and she turns around on the rack to look at him, and the rest of the sentence was going to be Youngstown and comes out: “Lupe’s. Open till three. Lupe doesn’t know anybody’s name.”

She laughs, startled, and swings her boots down. So they take the bike path west through the Grove instead of home and come out on Seacliff at the white truck. Lupe sees them coming, and the gold tooth shows, and two orders of carnitas come down out of the window in paper boats; nobody ordered. They eat standing up by the fender with La Flaca leaning on it, Lena with grease to her wrists, explaining with her mouth full that the pig is the most Catholic animal there is, because nothing on it goes to waste.
“Are you going to be okay?” he says. “At that table?”
Lena licks her thumb and thinks about it. “I’ll let you know.”

choices.text: Tell her what Thanksgiving is on Glenwood Avenue.
choices.key: Walking home at one in the morning, you told Lena what Thanksgiving is on Glenwood Avenue, and stopped before the end of the sentence.
response: So he tells her. His mother’s lasagna next to the turkey, because a turkey by itself is Protestant. Nonna’s cardoons fried in egg, which nobody under fifty will touch and everybody eats. Gina rolling her eyes at the kids’ table. Rosie’s place cards in crayon, a turkey on every one traced around her own hand, the fingers for feathers. The Lions losing in the front room, on schedule. And Danny’s chair, which his mother still sets, every year, with a plate and a glass, and nobody says anything about it.
Lena doesn’t ask about the chair. She listens to all of it as if she’s being invited.
He gets to the end and there’s one more sentence, and he stops short of it. She sees him stop, and lets him keep it.
“Are you going to be okay?” he says. “At that table?”
Lena thinks about it for most of a block. “I’ll let you know.”

response: He pushes the bike. She rides the rack another block and then gets down and walks beside him again, and they go into the Grove with the eucalyptus creaking overhead and dropping its bark in long curls on the path.

s23.slug: SUNDAY · 2:25 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DOOR
body: The card reader by Delgado’s front door has a red light that blinks once a second and turns everything near it faintly red: the glass, the bike rack, her hand going into the cardigan for her ID. Through the doors the lobby is bright and empty. A different night clerk tonight, a girl in a Marisol Crew sweatshirt, asleep with her cheek on her fist.

Jack locks La Flaca to the rack. When he straightens up Lena has her card out and isn’t swiping it yet. She stands at the door in the red light, very upright, with her shoulders back, the way she stands at Hale’s table before she takes someone apart.
“You’ve been a very good friend to me this week, Jack.”
She says it beautifully. Every word is in its place.

choices.text: “That’s the job.”
response: She nods, slowly, as if he has confirmed something she needed confirmed. Then she swipes her card, and the light goes green, and the lock lets go. “Goodnight,” she says, and goes in.

choices.text: “Goodnight, Magdalena.”
response: She stops with the card halfway to the reader.

She lets it stand. She doesn’t correct him and she doesn’t make anything of it; she just stands there in the red light with her whole name in the air between the bike rack and the glass, and then she swipes the card. “Goodnight, Jack.”

choices.text: Say nothing. Hold the door.
response: He says nothing. She swipes, the light goes green, and he pulls the door and holds it.

She goes through. He watches her cross the lobby past the sleeping clerk, the cardigan, the boots, one hand trailing along the top of the mailboxes as she goes, to the stairwell door; she opens it and turns on the first step and lifts her hand to him through the glass.

s24.slug: SUNDAY · 3:11 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAWN
body: At eleven minutes past three the alarm goes off in the voice the building keeps for this, and Delgado Hall comes out onto the lawn in what it sleeps in. The grass is wet and nearly cold, and three hundred people stand on it under the sodium lights one foot at a time, the way herons do, and with about the same opinion of it.

Theo comes down in the navy silk robe, flawless, with both bags off the top shelf of the closet, as always. Laney is in the PI LAM LITTLE shirt, which it turns out she also sleeps in, and one boot; she stands on the boot and hangs off Lena’s arm with the other foot tucked up under her. Lena is dressed, in the cardigan, over the same clothes she said goodnight in at the front door three-quarters of an hour ago. Priya has the clipboard and the air horn and has given up laminating anything about the lawn. Kevin is working his way down the line counting heads, his lips moving.

Margot comes out last, across the grass from the east door, with Theo’s camera still screwed to its tripod and the tripod over her shoulder like a rifle on parade. (“It’s insured,” Theo says, to anyone who looks at him.) She goes straight down the line with her Maglite. “Palms,” she says to each person. “Palms up.” Laney presents one, limp at the wrist, and asks Margot to read it. “Tell me I meet a dark stranger. Tell me he has a boat.” “I have been on the fourth-floor pull station since ten,” Margot tells her, “with a lens on it and Gold Bond on the handle. Whoever pulled it is standing on this lawn with one white hand.” Then a campus safety officer comes out of the lobby with the panel readout and says to Priya, “East stair,” and Margot stops walking.

“Picture it,” Theo says, in a whisper built to carry. “One woman. One camera. One night to catch him. Wrong *stairwell*.” Margot puts the Maglite on his face and leaves it there until he looks at his slippers.

At twenty to four the card is in Margot’s laptop in 305 with the overhead off: Margot in the desk chair, Theo standing because it’s his camera, Kevin standing because he can’t go to bed while there’s anybody left to count, and Jack.

On the screen is the fourth-floor lounge from the doorway, in the gray-green a camera makes of a room in the dark: the corner of the whiteboard, the lit panel of the vending machine, the red pull station on the far wall with its handle dusted white, a strip of carpet along the bottom of the frame, and at the right-hand edge the arm of the lounge chair with Margot’s hand on it, holding a pen. The clock in the corner runs. At 2:50 the hand on the chair arm opens and the pen rolls out of the picture. At 3:09 a bare heel and the corner of a pillow go across the bottom of the frame, left to right, and are gone. At 3:11 the picture shakes, and the hand jerks back into it.

Margot runs it back to 2:50 and stops it there, on her own open hand. She takes her glasses off and leans in close to the screen, and studies the hand like it belongs to somebody she’s going to have to interview.
“That’s REM,” Kevin offers. “It’s very normal. It happens to most people every night.”
“Not to me.” She puts the glasses back on. “I’m not writing it down.”
She takes the Moleskine out of the desk drawer and writes it down.

body.title: Margot’s Moleskine
body.text:
ALARM 4 · SUN 11/8 · 3:11 · EAST STAIR (NOT LOUNGE) · 26 DAYS
Observer asleep 2:50–3:11. First documented instance.

journal.title: The 3 a.m. alarm
journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log. Tuesday the 6th, nothing. Either the theory’s wrong or he’s on vacation. Alarm 3, Tuesday the 13th, 3:20, in a storm, under the overhang: twenty-five days. Margot says he’s irregular or he’s two people. Alarm 4, Sunday the 8th, 3:11: twenty-six days. Margot staked out the lounge pull station all night with Theo’s camera and Gold Bond on the handle. She fell asleep at 2:50 for the first time in recorded history. It came from the east stair.

body: At ten to eleven Sully’s is all television and no bell. The Saints are down fourteen to nothing at the end of the first quarter, and the brass ship’s bell hangs over the bar with its rope tied off to a cleat, and the owner stands under it in his Sully’s polo with his arms folded, a big pink man with nothing to do. A hundred people in black and gold are watching the screens and saying very little. The Bloody Mary bar has a line anyway.

Dale is on his stool at the end of the bar in the Barry Sanders jersey he wears as a vigil — the Lions are one and six — and he has made the bartender push two tables together under the fifth TV, because he has been told there are seven of them now.

Theo gets to the tables first, with a cocktail napkin on which he has drawn the seating in small square capitals, two rows of boxes and a name in each, COSTIGAN and BROUSSARD side by side at the end nearest the big screen. He sets it in the middle of the table like a menu. “Sight lines,” he says.

Lena picks it up. She studies it and thanks him for it, warmly, and borrows the pen clipped to Kevin’s quarter-zip and draws one neat arrow. “Becca goes by Jack,” she says. “It’s her first game. She needs somebody who can explain a nickel package without crying. I want Margot. Margot explains *America* to me during the commercials.” She hands the napkin back to Theo, improved.
“You’re very generous, Broussard,” says Theo, and arranges it in his breast pocket as a pocket square.
“It’s a potlatch,” Margot tells Kevin, not quietly enough. “They’re destroying property to establish rank.” Kevin passes her the fries.

Theo is on his feet before she reaches the table, pulling out the chair beside Jack’s. “Miss Lindell. Your first Saints game. We’ve given you the good seat, so everything after this is downhill.” Becca sits down beside Jack with an Abita root beer and her purse in her lap. She came straight from the six o’clock touch tank and smells faintly of the Marine Lab, salt and something with a great many legs, and this is her first Saints game and she wants it understood that she intends to learn. By the second quarter she has asked him what a nickel is twice and written it on a napkin once.
Carolina keeps running the ball up the middle. “That’s a lot of yards after contact,” Kevin says. “Clinically, that’s the tackling’s fault.”
At the half it’s seventeen to six, and Lena decides Becca has to learn the Who Dat.
“Don’t you *dare*,” says Laney.

“Hush, cher,” Lena says, and does it anyway, across the table, under her breath so as not to jinx the third quarter: where the breath goes, how the *dat* lands, why it isn’t a question. “You’re not asking anybody, Becca. You’re telling the room.” Becca listens with her chin up and says it back low, perfectly, the first time. “Oh!” she says. “It’s a *holler*. We have one for the cows.”
Lena’s phone lies face up beside her root beer the whole morning, and the name that used to send WHO DATTT before kickoff sends nothing.

On the fifth TV, at the edge of Jack’s eye, a promo comes on between plays, something bright and blue with water in it, and Theo, turning on his chair, says, “God. They’re still running that.” Jack is watching Lena show Becca where to put the breath.

Carolina kicks a field goal and it’s twenty to thirteen in the third. Then Brees steps up and throws it long down the right side, and Meachem catches it in stride with nobody near him and runs under the Superdome lights for fifty-four yards, and the owner yanks the rope off the cleat, and the bell goes, and the bar comes up out of its chairs. Becca is on her feet before any of them. *WHO DAT* — a half second ahead of the room, in a voice made for calling something in off a hillside a mile away — and the bar comes in a half second behind her, under it, as if she’d planned it. At the end of the bar Dale swivels clear around on his stool to see who that was. Kevin holds up a napkin: 10. Under it, smaller: *(early)*.
“She was *early*,” Laney tells Theo, scandalized. “Theodore, that girl just won the swimsuit round in a *Carhartt vest*.”

With five minutes left and Carolina driving, a Panther loses the ball at the goal line and Anthony Hargrove, a defensive tackle with no business near a football, picks it up and goes one yard with it into the end zone, which is as far as a defensive tackle is built to go. Lena is up on a chair at the bar end before the referee’s arms are up. The owner hands her the rope, and she rings the bell until he asks for it back, and then rings it again. “That’s *seven*!” she yells at Sully’s — the defense’s seventh touchdown of the year — and Sully’s, which didn’t know, cheers anyway.

At the two-minute warning she’s still down at the bar end on the rung of the chair, the rope in her fist; the owner has stopped asking. Becca leans over to Jack, practical, her napkin of football words folded in her hand. “Are you really doing three days on a Greyhound by yourself? For Thanksgiving?”

choices.text: “I’m going to ask Lena. So she doesn’t have to spend it across the table from him.”
choices.key: At Sully’s you told Becca you’re going to ask Lena to Youngstown for Thanksgiving.
response: “Oh, *good*,” Becca says. “She shouldn’t have to sit across from him.” She squeezes his arm. “Your mom will *love* her.” Then she draws a finger across her lips, a zipper, very firmly. “It’s yours to ask. I’m not *allowed*.”
Down at the bar end the field goal goes through, and Lena rings the bell for it, which isn’t allowed, and the owner allows it.

choices.text: “Just me and the Greyhound. I’ll read.”
response: “I’ll pack you a survival bag,” Becca says. She turns her napkin over and writes BUS — JACK across the top of the clean side, and underlines it.
Down at the bar end the field goal goes through, and Lena rings the bell for it, which isn’t allowed, and the owner allows it.

body: At twenty past one the Anacapa lot is bright and half empty, everybody either asleep or at the beach, and the sun comes back off the windshields in sheets. Eight and oh. Kevin has gone up to call his mother, and the Odyssey sits in its space with the back glass still reading WHO DAT · 7–0 in the white La Vang polish.

body.text: The seven is Jack’s, from Tuesday. It hasn’t improved with time. Lena gets the bottle and the remover out of the glove box and holds the polish out to him. “You did seven. You’re on the hook now.”
body.else: Lena gets the bottle and the remover out of the glove box and holds the polish out to him anyway. “Your turn, Youngstown.”

body: Becca stands beside them with her purse on her arm, reading the glass. “You guys keep *score*,” she says. “On the *car*.”

response: He takes the seven off with his thumb and the remover and writes an eight. It comes out leaning, the top loop bigger than the bottom, a snowman on its way down a hill.

response.text: Lena considers it with her head on one side. “I didn’t think you could do worse than your seven,” she says. “And look at you.”
response.else: Lena considers it with her head on one side. “Mine were better,” she says. “Give it a flag, at least.” He gives it a flag. It doesn’t help.

response: Becca takes the bottle like a diploma. She doesn’t stop at the seven. She wipes the glass clean with the remover and a Kleenex out of her purse and writes it all over again, WHO DAT · 8–0, in the capitals she letters Newman posters in, every letter the same height, and a flag at the end because she has seen Lena do it.
Lena screws the cap back onto the remover, tight, and hands it to Becca to keep. “Perfect,” she says.

s26.slug: SUNDAY · 4:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: At half past four the east stairwell has gone gray and cool, the sun on the far side of the building and nearly down into the water, and the fourth-floor landing still has the one bar of reception it has always had, provided Jack stands on the third step up and holds the RAZR toward the ceiling.
It’s half past seven on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up before it finishes ringing.
“Idaho!” she says. “Your *girlfriend*!”

body.text: Gina saw it on the Facebook on Wednesday, it turns out, at the kitchen table, and had told the house inside of four minutes, Nonna twice. “Four days,” his mother says. “I have to hear it from your sister’s computer.”
body.else: Becca’s card came yesterday, it turns out, on the cow stationery — a thank-you for his mother’s thank-you note, two cows drawn at the bottom — and it’s on the refrigerator under the St. Brigid’s magnet. It doesn’t say anything, exactly. His mother reads him all of it anyway, and then reads him the end again, where Becca signed it *Love, Becca*. “A girl doesn’t write *love* to the mother,” she says, “unless.”

body: “Is she coming for Thanksgiving? Bring her! Nonna wants to see the girl who writes on cows.”
“She’s going home to Idaho, Ma.”
“Then Christmas! Bring her at Christmas. I’ll make the cardoons.”

Jack says that’s nice of her, and that he’ll ask, and that Becca would like the cardoons. His mother says of course she’ll like the cardoons, everybody likes the cardoons, and then she wants to know about the bus. Three days. He’ll come in the door smelling like a bus.
There’s a click on the line, and the hiss of the extension in the upstairs hall, and somebody breathing, and then Nonna. “E la ragazza?”
Which one, Jack doesn’t ask. Nonna doesn’t say. The extension clicks off again.
His mother’s voice comes back lower, for one sentence. “Your father’s in the garage a lot.” Then it’s her regular voice again, asking if he’s eating.

choices.text: “We’ll see, Ma.”
response: “That’s your father’s,” his mother says. “Don’t you start.”

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say.

choices.text: “A friend from school might come for Thanksgiving. Lena.”
choices.key: On the phone you told your mother a friend from school might come for Thanksgiving. Lena.
response: His mother draws in a breath you could hear in Akron. “The veil girl? Gina’s friend, from the Facebook? Doesn’t she have a *fidanzato*?”
“Not anymore, Ma.”
“And Idaho doesn’t mind?”
“Idaho’s going to Idaho.”
His mother takes a moment with that. “Then I want both,” she says. “One at Thanksgiving, one at Christmas. One at a time, like a civilized family.”

Jack turns the front half of it into English in his head, a word behind her — *who leaves the old road for the new knows what he leaves* — and stops there.
“Giacomino,” Nonna says, fond, and hangs up on him by accident, and on his mother too, who was still on the kitchen phone.

s27.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Be Not Afraid”
body: At nine the blue glass on the west wall is only black, and all of St. Brendan’s light is on the inside: the sanctuary lamp, the votives racked red by the Marian shrine, the lamps let down from the ribs of the ceiling on their long chains. The Book of the Dead stands open on its lectern beside the shrine, a week fuller than it was on Monday.

Jack has already been to Mass for this Sunday, last night at five. He came back for the names. Becca is on his left in her coat with her keys in the pocket for after — an early lab, and Becca has never been on time when early was available. Lena is on his right, faintly bay leaf; the Sunday soup went down to the Harbor Inn at seven in Kevin’s Odyssey.

Kevin is lector, in a tie under the navy quarter-zip, and he reads Elijah and the widow of Zarephath in his clear team-captain voice: the jar of flour shall not go empty, nor the jug of oil run dry. *Do not be afraid.*

At the Prayers of the Faithful he comes back to the ambo with the red ledger itself, and reads the November names the way they were written, steadily, one after another down the ruled lines. *Margaret Dwyer.* *Abuelita Rosa and Abuelo Chuy Ortega.* *Father Patrick Kelleher.* *Captain Joe Silva, of the* Marisol Rose, *lost at sea.* *Lucille Guidry.* *Nora Calloway.* *Antonio Rinaldi.* And under that, in the same steady voice, *Nora Calloway* again.

Jack hears his grandfather’s name said out loud in a church in California, by a kid from San Jose, to a few hundred people who have never heard of Black Monday, and the church answers it with all the others. *Lord, hear our prayer.* He’ll write Danny tonight that it got said.

At the first *Nora Calloway* Lena turns in the pew to look toward the back, and Jack looks with her. Julian Park-Ellis is standing just inside the doors with his guitar case at his feet, in a cardigan, his hands folded in front of him. He doesn’t come any farther in. Lena turns back around.

After the names Gus brings the organ up under the choir, and they sing “Be Not Afraid.” Becca sings every verse from memory, in tune and full out, and on his other side Lena takes the alto line under it.
When Jack goes up for Communion, the place inside the doors is empty.

s27a.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD WALL
body: After, the courtyard is cold and nearly dark. The only light comes out of the side door in a long yellow slant across the flagstones, and the olive tree stands half in it, its leaves gone silver on the lit side. Somebody has finally shut the broken sprinkler off at the valve; the planter just drips. Becca kissed Jack’s cheek on the steps and was across Ocean Road to the Ranger by two minutes past ten with her keys already out.
Lena sits up on the low wall with her boots hanging, and Jack sits beside her. She tells it like it happened to somebody else.

“He found me on Facebook Tuesday,” she says. “Everybody does, eventually.” She opened the laptop this morning for the first time all week, she says, and there he was, three messages down, under two of her aunts. “He asked if I’d come Thursday. To Bastille. To hear the new one. It wasn’t ready last week; he pushed it to this one.” She knocks one boot heel against the stones. “He said you promised to stay to the end.”

body.text: Then she takes her license out of her back pocket and slides his card from behind it, and holds it out, and he takes hers out of *Big Sur* and gives it back. Each of them puts their own away.
Then she takes her license out of her back pocket and slides his card out from behind hers, and taps it twice on his knee before she gives it back.

response: “Good,” Lena says. “He thinks everybody leaves in the second chorus.” She pulls the cardigan closed at her throat and sits a while longer on the cold wall with him, swinging her boots, talking about nothing — Mémère’s fruitcake, the Panthers’ running back, whether Kevin owns a tie or borrowed one.

response: Lena laughs, and the courtyard gives it back. “Then he’ll have one person in the room on the beat,” she says. “The wrong beat. But on it.”

response: Lena looks at him in the yellow from the side door. “I think I will,” she says.

body: At twenty to midnight 412 is the desk lamp bent down low over Jack’s bed and nothing else. Theo is turned to the wall with the silk robe over the back of his chair, and he hasn’t moved since eleven. Jack sits against the cinderblock with a yellow legal pad on his knee. Danny’s letter is open on the blanket beside him, out of the Carhartt’s inside pocket, worn white along the folds from a week in the Carhartt.
He has the first part done.

body.title: Legal pad
body.text:
D —
Saints 8–0. Down 14 after one quarter and won it on a fumble return by a defensive tackle. Lena rang the bell. Browns had the bye. I’m told it went well.
Nonno’s in the book. They read the names tonight at the 9:00. A guy from down the hall read it out loud — Antonio Rinaldi, in California, in front of everybody. I was there for it. That one was yours.
Which leaves the margin. Up the side of Danny’s page in pencil, squeezed in after the D: ABOUT TIME. WHAT’D SHE SAY BACK. Jack clicks the pen.
body.else: Which leaves the line from Michaelmas he still hasn’t answered: *You sound happy out there.* Jack clicks the pen.

choices.text: “She said hey back. She said it like she meant it. That’s all you get, jagoff.”
response: He writes it exactly as he’d say it to Danny’s face, and leaves it as it came out. Danny will laugh at *jagoff*. It was his word first.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it.

choices.text: The truth: “Her boyfriend broke up with her. I’m with Becca now. Officially. I’m doing it right, D.”
choices.key: In your letter to Danny you told him the truth: Lena’s single, and you’re with Becca, officially.
response: He writes it in one go, and lets it stand.

body: At eight minutes to twelve the RAZR goes off against the blanket, one short buzz, and the outer screen lights blue: LENA.

body.text: Ask me again in a week. —L.

body: He holds it open on his knee beside the legal pad. Across the room Theo doesn’t stir. Jack thumbs *i will* into the keypad a letter at a time, and sends it, and shuts the phone, and sets the legal pad down on the floor by the bed.
Then he picks it up again. The letter is half a page short of done, and there’s room at the bottom, and Danny reads to the bottom of everything.
